title: Damage Assessment Cards.
subtitle: Dealers on CarMax Auctions couldn't tell how bad a vehicle's damage was before bidding. We redesigned how the vehicle detail page shows it, so they can judge the damage at a glance and bid with confidence.

glance.Problem: Damage photos on the vehicle detail page were too small and too spread out for dealers to judge before bidding.
glance.Contribution: Product design on a two-person team, with Bobby Eaves as lead.
glance.Outcome: A vertical stack of damage cards: a large photo with the damage highlighted, plus its location, type and size.

hero.alt: Damage assessment cards on a CarMax Auctions vehicle detail page, each with a large photo, the damaged area highlighted, and a label for location, type and size
hero.caption: Final design: damage assessment cards on the vehicle detail page

sections.label: Problem
sections.heading: Is this damage worth the bid?
paras: On the vehicle detail page, dealers had trouble judging how bad the damage was before bidding. The damage photos were too small, and the wide spacing made the details hard to follow. That slowed down the main decision the page exists for: is this damage worth the bid?

image.alt: The original vehicle assessment list: one damage row with a small thumbnail of the car, the location "Front Left Door", "Dented", and a "6 to 8 inches" tag spread far apart
image.caption: Before: a small thumbnail and wide spacing made each damage hard to judge

sections.label: Context
sections.heading: Each competitor solved part of it.
paras: This was an April 2026 study on damage clarity in vehicle assessment. I looked at three competitors, and each one solved part of the problem but not all of it:
bullets: ACV has descriptive damage callouts, but they aren't visually tied to the photos, so users have to scan back and forth.
Manheim uses images too small to read at a glance.
Openlane has a diagram that shows where the damage is, but not what it actually looks like.

sections.label: Exploration
sections.heading: Two layouts made the cut.
paras: The team explored several layouts and narrowed them to two:
bullets: Option A: a large photo with the damage highlighted and details underneath.
Option B: a compact thumbnail with the details beside it.

sections.label: Research
sections.heading: What customers are saying.
quotes: I would have never known there was a missing piece…
I like that it's zoomed in and I like the little description at the bottom. It tells you exactly what it is.
Vertical scrolling feels natural because it's how people already scroll social media.

sections.label: Solution
sections.heading: A vertical stack of damage cards.
paras: We went with Option A: a vertically scrolling stack of damage cards. Each card has a large photo with the damage highlighted, plus a short label showing location, type, and size (for example, “Front – Bumper Cover · Dented · 6–8 inches”). It works on any device and gives dealers what they need to bid with confidence, without hunting across the page.

image.alt: Final damage card: a large photo of a front bumper with the dent outlined in orange, labeled "Front – Bumper Cover, Dented, 6–8 inches"
image.caption: The final card: large photo, highlighted damage, and location, type and size

results: preferred the larger image with supporting details below (n=50).
nextSteps: Ship Option A and measure whether it changes bid confidence or how fast dealers decide.
Run a follow-up on horizontal vs. vertical scrolling. The interview sample (5 people) is small next to the survey (50).
Test how the cards hold up on vehicles with many damage points, since a long vertical list could get heavy.
